passage:
The farewell party in the Pune flat ran late, rain was hammering down, and the last bus had gone. A few drinks in, Jatin felt brilliant: funnier, louder, sure everyone loved his jokes. When Parul laughed at one, he read it as interest and kept draping his arm round her shoulders, even after she shifted away twice. Then he announced he'd ride his scooter home in the rain. "I'm totally fine." It sounded completely reasonable to him.
His friend Samar took the keys. "Not tonight. You're sleeping on my sofa."
In the grey morning, head pounding, Jatin replayed the evening. Parul hadn't been flirting; she'd been polite, and he had made her uncomfortable. And the scooter, in that rain. His stomach turned. He messaged her: "I'm sorry about last night. I crossed a line."

qa.q: Who took Jatin's scooter keys?
qa.a: His friend Samar took the keys.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel while drinking?
qa.a: Jatin felt brilliant and bold, sure everyone loved his jokes.

qa.q: What was the wise step at the party, and what did Jatin do the next morning?
qa.a: Samar took the keys so Jatin wouldn't ride in the rain; the next morning Jatin admitted crossing a line and apologised to Parul.

qa.q: How did the evening feel for Parul?
qa.a: Parul was uncomfortable, shifting away twice while Jatin misread her politeness as interest.

grounding: A young person who has been drinking feels bolder, misreads someone's politeness and plans a risky ride that seems reasonable at the time.

passage:
At his cousin's sangeet on a Jaipur rooftop, Yash had been drinking steadily since eight. The music was loud and everything felt easy. When a friend joked that no one could climb the water-tank ladder in the dark, Yash was already pulling off his jacket. "Watch me." The ladder was wet from the evening wash. In the moment, it seemed a perfectly sensible idea.
His cousin Sarika grabbed his arm. "Yash. Look at me. You can't even walk straight."
"I'm fine!" he said, too loudly, and swayed.
Sarika didn't argue further. She steered him to a chair, pushed a glass of water into his hand and stayed beside him. Much later, clearer-headed, he looked at the slick, rusty ladder and went pale. "Why did that seem like a good idea?"

qa.q: What did a friend joke that no one could climb?
qa.a: The water-tank ladder in the dark.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when he looked at the ladder later?
qa.a: Yash felt shaken and shocked, going pale and wondering why it had seemed a good idea.

qa.q: Which of Sarika's choices kept Yash safe?
qa.a: Sarika grabbed his arm, didn't argue further, sat him down with water and stayed beside him.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt watching Yash pull off his jacket?
qa.a: Sarika was probably alarmed, seeing that Yash couldn't walk straight and was heading for a wet ladder.

grounding: Drinking makes a young person bolder and less careful, so a dangerous dare feels reasonable in the moment.

passage:
Dear Jatin,
I owe you an apology for Saturday.
After three drinks at Rhea's party, I felt amazing: brave, funny, like nothing could go wrong. I teased you in front of everyone about failing the driving test. I thought you were laughing along. Looking back, you weren't laughing. You were quiet, and you left early. I just didn't see it.
Then I nearly got on the back of Karan's bike, even though he'd been drinking more than me. At the time it seemed totally reasonable. You were the one who texted, 'Don't. I'm booking you a cab.' I was annoyed. Now I'm grateful.
The drinks made every bad idea feel like a good one. I'm sorry I hurt you. Can we get chai this week?
Aadhya

qa.q: Whose party was it?
qa.a: Rhea's party.

qa.q: What did Aadhya feel after three drinks?
qa.a: Aadhya felt amazing, brave and funny, as if nothing could go wrong.

qa.q: What went wrong at the party, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Aadhya misread Jatin's silence and nearly rode with a drunk rider; Jatin's cab booking kept Aadhya safe, and the letter begins to repair the hurt.

qa.q: How might Jatin have felt at the party?
qa.a: Jatin probably felt embarrassed and hurt by the teasing, and worried about Aadhya getting on the bike.

grounding: Shows a young person who, after drinking, feels bolder and less careful, misreads a friend's reaction and nearly takes a risk that felt reasonable at the time.

passage: Payal, you remember the wedding in Siliguri, right? I'm Anirban, and I still cringe. After the sangeet, the cousins had a few drinks on the terrace. I had more than a few. I felt ten feet tall. Then someone said the pond behind the hall looked perfect for a midnight swim. In my head, that was the best idea anyone had ever had. I was already taking off my shoes. You were standing there with this worried face, and I actually thought you were daring me. You weren't. You grabbed my arm and said, 'Anirban, it's dark and you can't swim straight.' I argued, loudly. You didn't let go. Next morning I saw that pond in daylight: weeds, broken glass, deep in the middle. The drinks made it feel like fun. It could have been the end.

qa.q: Where was the wedding?
qa.a: In Siliguri.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel after the drinks on the terrace?
qa.a: Anirban felt ten feet tall, bold and sure that swimming in the pond was a great idea.

qa.q: What does Anirban's story show about drinking and decisions?
qa.a: Drinking made a dangerous idea feel reasonable and made Anirban misread Payal's worry as a dare.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt holding on to Anirban?
qa.a: Payal was probably frightened for Anirban and determined, even through the loud arguing.

grounding: Shows a young person who after drinking feels bold and careless about risk, misreads a friend's worried face, and nearly acts on a bad idea that felt reasonable.

passage:
Saturday night: At a flat party in Gangtok, Dolma had several drinks and felt brilliant. Loud, funny, invincible. At two, she grabbed her car keys. 'I'm fine to drive. It's five minutes.' Her friend Asif took the keys out of her hand. 'You're not. We're taking a taxi.' Dolma was furious and called him a killjoy.
Sunday: She woke with a headache and a sick feeling as she remembered. She'd been sure she was fine. She wasn't.
The following Saturday: At the next party, Dolma left her car at home and told Asif, 'If I start saying anything is a great idea after midnight, stop me.' He laughed. She had one drink, danced, and took the taxi home with him.

qa.q: Where was the party on Saturday night?
qa.a: At a flat in Gangtok.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel on Sunday morning?
qa.a: She felt sick and ashamed as she remembered trying to drive.

qa.q: What did Dolma change by the following Saturday?
qa.a: She left her car at home, had one drink and asked Asif to stop her if she started getting bold ideas.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt when Dolma called him a killjoy?
qa.a: He was probably hurt but sure he was right, caring more about her safety than her approval.

grounding: Shows a young person who after drinking feels bold and careless, believes driving is reasonable, and learns how alcohol makes bad decisions feel sensible.

subtopic: Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and other substances
passage: Gopika, you're off to that farewell party tonight, so let your Urmila Bua tell you something from when I was twenty. College fest, a friend's rooftop, and someone kept filling my cup. After the third one I felt clever and brave. I told a senior, loudly, that his poetry was rubbish. A boy from the next flat asked us to turn the music down, and I was sure he was joking, so I turned it up. And when Rakesh, who had been drinking more than me, offered to ride me home on his scooter, it sounded like a perfectly fine idea. My friend Hema pulled me back, said no, and called her father to fetch us both. Next morning I couldn't believe that girl on the roof was me. It all felt sensible at the time. That's exactly the danger, Gopika.

qa.q: Who offered to take Urmila home on a scooter?
qa.a: Rakesh, who had been drinking more than her.

qa.q: How did young Urmila feel after the third cup, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: She felt bold and clever, which led her to insult a senior's poetry and misread the neighbour's request as a joke.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned the night toward safety?
qa.a: Hema refused to let Urmila ride with Rakesh and called her father to fetch them both.

qa.q: How might the boy who asked them to lower the music have felt?
qa.a: He likely felt ignored and annoyed when they turned it up instead.

grounding: Illustrates how drinking at a party made a young person bolder, louder and careless about risk, misreading a request and nearly accepting a dangerous ride.
